title: Lesotho: Youth, the Fragile but Indispensable Engine of the National Economy
excerpt: With over 60% of Lesotho's people under 30, young workers are key to diversifying the economy, but unemployment, precarious jobs and skills gaps hold them back.
seo_title: Lesotho: Youth, the Fragile but Vital Engine of the Economy
seo_desc: Over 60% of Basotho are under 30, but unemployment above 35% and precarious work limit their role in Lesotho's economy.
image_alt: Young workers in Lesotho, where youth employment is central to the national economy
body_html:
Maseru, 16 November 2025—PRESS AFRICA—In the heart of the southern African mountains, Lesotho is increasingly betting on its youth to revive an economy in search of diversification. With a population of which more than 60% is under 30, the small kingdom enclaved within South Africa has a major demographic asset. But the contribution of this young workforce to the economy remains hampered by unemployment, precarity and a lack of technical training.

A large but underemployed youth

According to data from the Lesotho Bureau of Statistics (BOS), young people make up nearly two-thirds of the working population, but more than 35% of them are unemployed. Many work in informal jobs in agriculture, tailoring or small-scale urban trade.

"The potential of our youth is considerable, but it is still underused. We must turn this energy into a productive force," said Thabo Sofonia, Minister of Labour and Employment, at the Maseru economic forum last October.

The formal sector, dominated by the textile industry, subsistence agriculture and remittances from migrant workers in South Africa, is struggling to absorb the thousands of young graduates entering the labor market each year.

Textiles, the leading employer of young people

For two decades, Lesotho has been one of the main garment exporters in sub-Saharan Africa, notably to the United States thanks to the AGOA trade agreement. The garment factories, concentrated in the capital Maseru and in the industrial zones of Maputsoe, employ nearly 40,000 people, more than 70% of whom are young women.

This sector is a genuine lifeline of jobs for young people, but working conditions are often precarious: low wages, no social protection and dependence on fluctuations in the international market.

"We work hard, but our income does not always allow us to meet our needs," says ’Makhotso, 24, a worker in a garment factory in Maputsoe.

Agriculture, the forgotten pillar of rural youth

In rural areas, where more than half of the population still lives, subsistence farming remains the main economic activity. Young people play an essential role in producing maize, wheat and vegetables.

However, the sector's low profitability, climate change and lack of access to credit hold back their engagement. The government is trying to steer young people toward agribusiness and modern farming cooperatives, through the "Youth Agripreneur Lesotho" program, launched in 2023 with the support of the African Development Bank.

"The future of our country lies in innovative agriculture, run by young people trained in new technologies," says ’Mathato Molapo, the program's coordinator.

Migration and the weight of remittances

Historically, thousands of young Basotho have emigrated to neighboring South Africa, notably to work in the gold and platinum mines. Although this migration has declined since the decline of South Africa's mining sector, migrant remittances still account for nearly 15% of national GDP.

This income plays a vital role in household consumption and children's education, but dependence on it makes the economy vulnerable to external shocks.

Entrepreneurship and training: levers of renewal

Faced with a lack of formal jobs, more and more young people are turning to entrepreneurship. Local start-ups are emerging in digital technology, recycling and crafts, often supported by incubators such as the Bacha Entrepreneurship Project.

The government, for its part, has expanded vocational training programs through the National Training Centre for Technical Skills, in order to equip young people with the skills needed in construction, mechanics and renewable energy.

Despite these efforts, economic analysts believe the transition to a more inclusive economy will take time. "Lesotho must turn its youth into productive human capital. That requires an education policy adapted to the market and a better business climate," stresses Dr. Palesa Mokete, an economist at the National University of Lesotho.

A future to build

Lesotho's young workforce is both its greatest wealth and its greatest challenge. If properly supervised, trained and integrated, it could become the engine of sustainable, diversified growth. But without sufficient investment in education, technology and rural infrastructure, there is a real risk of an entire generation remaining on the margins of economic development.

Writer: Saïd TESSILIMI
